title: J.P. Morgan Private Bank Appoints Keeve Tan as Taiwan Market Head - East & Partners
content: (11 November 2026 – Taiwan) J.P. Morgan Private Bank has named Keeve Tan as Taiwan Market Head, effective January 2027, strengthening its leadership team in Asia. Based in Hong Kong, Tan will report to Harshika Patel, Chief Executive Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Bank in Asia, and oversee the bank’s Taiwan business, serving clients through its offshore private banking platforms in Hong Kong and Singapore. Tan will succeed the current market head, who is departing after more than 19 years with the bank to spend more time with family. The outgoing executive will work alongside Tan and the regional leadership team to facilitate a smooth transition. Tan brings nearly two decades of experience spanning private banking, global markets and trading, with extensive expertise in Taiwan and Greater China. He joins from Bank of Singapore, where he served as Managing Director and APAC Market Head, leading the private banking business serving Taiwanese clients. His responsibilities included business strategy, client acquisition and talent development. Earlier in his career, Tan held senior roles at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation (OCBC) and United Overseas Bank (UOB), gaining experience across futures, foreign exchange, derivatives and global markets. The agreement aligns with the bank’s broader AI strategy of leveraging advanced technologies to enhance efficiency, accelerate innovation and strengthen operational resilience. The collaboration could accelerate JPMorgan’s technology transformation by streamlining software development and automating routine tasks. Codex will likely enable engineers to improve coding efficiency, reduce development timelines and allocate resources toward more complex projects. Broader adoption of AI-powered tools is also likely to enhance employee productivity and optimize workflows, potentially supporting operating leverage over time. Cybersecurity represents another strategic opportunity. Given the bank’s extensive digital infrastructure and sensitive customer data, enhanced cybersecurity defenses will support operational resilience and reinforce customer confidence. However, AI-generated outputs will require rigorous validation and human oversight. Despite these potential benefits, the collaboration could further increase JPM’s technology-related expenses. With the bank planning to spend $19.8 billion on technology this year, additional costs associated with AI integration, computing infrastructure, employee training and ongoing model monitoring could add to its expense burden, potentially delaying the realization of meaningful efficiency gains. title: J.P. Morgan Report, CoreWeave Earnings Provide Positive Signals For Data Center Construction In 2027 - Bisnow
content:
While the midterm election results sent a clear message that voters have concerns about the rapid data center build-out, it appears the industry's construction pipeline is still on track — at least for next year. New research from J.P. Morgan Asset Management and comments from CoreWeave leadership in the wake of its unexpectedly strong third-quarter earnings report point to a positive outlook for development in 2027, even if the sector is ultimately expected to lose steam in 2028. “We do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that’s occurred,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during the firm’s Tuesday afternoon earnings call. “We are very comfortable with our pipeline. ... We believe that what has occurred is a statement around how you build. We want to build responsibly.” “So we think that is an opportunity for us to continue to scale our business within the new political reality that exists,” he added. The AI firm's stock had plunged last week after anti-data center candidates swept the midterms, but it has been rallying since then, including a more than 26% jump since the earnings report was released Tuesday. CoreWeave reported $3.66B in quarterly revenue, up 168% year-over-year and beating industry estimates of $3.56B. It has also raised its full-year revenue guidance. The bullish outlook aligns with a projection from J.P. Morgan, which expects artificial intelligence-related capital expenditures to reach $1.5T in 2027 and level off in the following year due to political pushback, Semafor reported. J.P. Morgan researchers said in the report that the legislative pushback to data center construction has “more bark than bite.” Of the 16 statewide moratoriums that have been proposed, just one in New York has become law. The report also found that weeding out speculative projects could be good for the industry. It said of the 430 gigawatts worth of proposed data center projects, just 59% are in active development. “Projects already under construction are generally less vulnerable to new restrictions,” J.P. Morgan Global Market Strategist Stephanie Aliaga wrote. “Future developments face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing, with delays and higher costs potentially pressuring returns.” Contact

ATLANTA, Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Expression Therapeutics, Inc., a clinical-stage company developing investigational stem cell and gamma delta (γδ) T-cell therapies, today announced that Chief Executive Officer David F. Townson, Ph.D., has been invited to attend the 45th Annual J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, January 11-14, 2027, in San Francisco. During the week, Dr. Townson will meet with prospective pharmaceutical partners about the company's hemophilia A and neuroendocrine tumor programs. J.P. Morgan hosts the conference each January. The firm describes the invitation-only event as the largest healthcare investment symposium in the industry, bringing together industry leaders, emerging companies, technology developers and the investment community. Hemophilia A programExpression Therapeutics' lead program is an investigational, one-time therapy for hemophilia A that modifies a patient's own blood stem cells to produce factor VIII. In a Phase 1 study (NCT05265767) published in the New England Journal of Medicine, all patients with severe hemophilia A treated after myeloablative conditioning had an annualized bleeding rate of zero over a combined 81 months of follow-up. Long-term follow-up presented at this year's ASGCT annual meeting demonstrated durable efficacy through the most recent time point of four years. FDA granted the program Fast Track, Orphan Drug, and Rare Pediatric Disease Designations in April 2026, and the company plans to open a potentially registrational U.S. Phase 2 study in Q4 2027. Neuroendocrine tumor programsNeuroendocrine neoplasms are rising in incidence in the U.S., where an estimated 244,000 people are living with a diagnosis made in the prior 20 years. Once these tumors spread, approved systemic therapies mainly slow growth. In the NETTER-1 Phase 3 trial, LUTATHERA® produced an objective response rate of only 18%. The company's two preclinical cell therapies engineer a patient's own gamma delta T cells to secrete a CD3-engaging protein inside the tumor. The design aims to concentrate T-cell activity at the tumor and limit exposure elsewhere in the body. ET401 targets SSTR2, the receptor physicians already use to image and treat well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. In laboratory studies at Emory University's Winship Cancer Institute, ET401 cells reduced the viability of tumor spheroids derived from a patient's tumor more than unmodified gamma delta T cells did (unpublished company data). The company plans to submit an Investigational New Drug application for ET401 in Q4 2027. ET501 targets PTK7 and is intended for poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma and pediatric neuroblastoma, with an IND planned for Q1 2029. As previously reported, NCI SBIR within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has awarded the company a Phase II grant to advance the program to IND. U.S. manufacturingExpression Therapeutics manufactures its viral vectors and cell therapies at its own 43,000-square-foot GMP facility in Cincinnati, Ohio. "JPM week puts the decision-makers in pharmaceutical partnering in one place for four days," said Dr. Townson. "We are bringing published clinical data demonstrating durable safety and efficacy for ET3, three FDA designations and our own U.S. manufacturing. We want to meet partners who can help us move our hemophilia A program through Phase 2 and our oncology programs into the clinic." About Expression TherapeuticsExpression Therapeutics, Inc., based in Atlanta, Georgia, is a clinical-stage biotechnology company advancing an investigational autologous stem cell therapy for hemophilia A and investigational cell therapies for neuroendocrine tumors and neuroblastoma. The company manufactures its therapies at its U.S.-based GMP facility in Cincinnati, Ohio. None of the company's product candidates has been approved by the FDA or any other regulatory authority. Emirates NBD, described as a leading banking group in the Mena region, has signed an agreement with JP Morgan Asset Management aimed at advancing and developing digital wealth and investment solutions for its customers, according to Trade Arabia. The memorandum of understanding establishes a framework for the two organizations to explore making JP Morgan Asset Management's active exchange-traded funds available through Emirates NBD's digital wealth architecture, which would broaden investor access to diversified international markets. The initiative also seeks to strengthen investor education and engagement through jointly curated content, market insights and interactive digital tools. The arrangement combines Emirates NBD's regional footprint and expanding digital wealth capabilities with JP Morgan Asset Management's global investment expertise and active ETF offering. Raed AlJaser, Head of Wealth Management at Emirates NBD, indicated that the collaboration is part of the bank's continued development of its digital wealth proposition. He said the two sides aim to connect regional demand with global market opportunities, improve the digital customer experience and give customers the intelligence needed to pursue their financial goals. Although JPMorgan did publish this figure, it came from a November 2025 report by a team led by Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou on MSCI’s earlier digital-asset proposal, which MSCI ultimately didn’t implement. MSCI then updated its rules on October 15 to make “non-operating companies” ineligible for its global indexes. Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) trades at $73,899, down 0.6% in the last 24 hours and 5.6% over the past week. Meanwhile, Strategy’s shares trade at $123 in premarket, up 1.8% for the day but down 9.1% for the week and 18.9% for the year. When a benchmark removes a stock, passive index funds tracking it must sell, because those funds automatically hold whatever the benchmark lists. JPMorgan’s $2.8 billion estimate means these funds would sell Strategy shares to other investors, while the company’s 850,364 BTC, valued at around $63 billion, would remain on its balance sheet. JPMorgan also noted that an additional $8.8 billion could leave if other index providers follow MSCI’s lead. Strategy has contested the size of this impact since MSCI moved to drop it. The company said in August that funds tracking MSCI’s global indexes hold about 13 million shares, or 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding, which it considers less than a single day’s trading volume. At a share price of $123, those 13 million shares would be worth around $1.6 billion, well below JPMorgan’s earlier $2.8 billion estimate. Strategy operates two lines of business. Its traditional analytics software division generated $125.4 million in revenue during the third quarter, while its Bitcoin treasury is funded from outside sources. These include an at-the-market (ATM) program, which gradually sells new shares in the daily market, and five series of preferred stock that pay fixed dividends before common shareholders. The ATM program raised $5.41 billion in net proceeds during the third quarter. JPMorgan analysts highlighted funding concerns, saying removal from the index could raise questions about Strategy’s ability to raise equity or debt. A lower share price means any shares sold through the ATM buy less Bitcoin. Strategy is also reporting a BTC Yield of negative 3.7% for 2026, meaning each share holds less Bitcoin than at the start of the year. Michael Saylor, Strategy’s executive chairman, said on February 5 that the company doesn’t sell equity when its stock trades weakly. About STRC, its primary preferred stock, he added, “If it trades below 100, we don’t sell them.” With STRC below its $100 stated amount, two of Strategy’s funding sources could slow down at the same time. In the week to November 8, the company also spent more on share buybacks than on Bitcoin. Strategy has also sold approximately $432 million of Bitcoin through the third quarter to cover preferred dividends and fund STRC buybacks, according to its third-quarter 8-K report. A Strategy MSCI exit would directly hit Strategy shareholders but only indirectly affect Bitcoin. Selling Strategy stock moves shares between investors without touching the company’s 850,364 BTC, so Bitcoin feels the effect only through how fast Strategy buys. Other factors are also weighing on Bitcoin, as U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs posted net outflows of $95 million on November 10, a fourth consecutive day of outflows. Strategy’s weekly 8-K filings after November 30 could show where the selling goes. If they show new Bitcoin purchases, the index selling stayed inside the stock. However, if they show Strategy drawing on its $1.25 billion sale authority beyond what dividends require, the selling has reached Bitcoin, giving Bitcoin’s price a clear reason to come under pressure. title: J.P. Morgan names new head of Asia equity strategy - finews.asia
content: J.P. Morgan Private Bank has appointed Cameron Chui as its new head of equity strategy for Asia, expanding the Hong Kong-based investment strategist’s leadership role as the bank strengthens its equity capabilities across the region. Cameron Chui will take up the position in November 2026 and report to Christopher Baggini, global head of equity strategy. He succeeds Timothy Fung, who has moved to a new role as an investor on the private bank’s China team. In his new role, Chui will lead the Private Bank’s equity strategy team in Asia and oversee the development of the firm’s equity views and investment recommendations across the region. He will work with the global equity strategy and investment teams to assess markets, sectors and individual stocks and translate the firm’s highest-conviction views into investment insights for clients. Chui joined J.P. Morgan in 2019 and has been a member of the Equity Strategy team. Before joining the firm, he was a global equity portfolio manager, managing portfolios focused on U.S., European and U.K. equities. His experience investing across global markets, alongside his knowledge of Asia, will bring a broader perspective to the role, J.P. Morgan said. “Cameron’s promotion reflects our belief in leadership continuity and our commitment to recognizing exceptional talent within the firm,” Baggini said. He added that Chui’s understanding of Asian markets and global investment experience would be valuable as investment opportunities across the region become “increasingly differentiated.” Fung led the Private Bank’s Equity Strategy team for five years, during which he strengthened its equity advisory capabilities and investment insights for clients, the company writes. He will now work as an investor within the China team.

title: A brighter productivity outlook for the AI era - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. AI’s promise is becoming real. As the technology races forward, trillions of dollars are flowing into semiconductors, data centers and power suppliers – the new AI ecosystem. But will AI make the economy more productive and, if so, by how much, how quickly and for whom? No force has a greater impact on our Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMAs) than productivity growth, the pace at which an economy turns its labor and capital into more output. Productivity underpins economic growth, living standards, corporate earnings, inflation and interest rates. As the economist Paul Krugman once said, “Productivity isn’t everything, but in the long run, it is almost everything.” We believe AI will raise productivity meaningfully and durably over our 10- to 15-year horizon, reshaping the nature of work and patterns of investment. While we have incrementally incorporated AI’s potential into our LTCMAs since 2023, the dramatic acceleration in capabilities and investment now requires more sophisticated analysis. To capture that shift, we have rebuilt our AI methodology and embedded it within our macroeconomic building blocks. Anchored around a Cobb-Douglas production function, it attributes an economy’s output to its labor and capital, and how efficiently those are used (see Methodology Handbook). In that framework, AI lifts labor productivity, measured as output per hour worked, through two channels. First, it makes existing work more efficient, enabling the same people and machines to produce more (total factor productivity, or TFP). Second, it equips workers with improved tools, systems and infrastructure as investment scales (capital deepening).[1] Here, we present our new methodology and the insight it delivers. Source: Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin et al., “GPTs are GPTs: Labor Market Impact Potential of LLMs,” Science, June 2024; J.P. Morgan Asset
Management. *Exposure is defined as AI reducing the time to complete a task by at least 50% at equivalent quality. **LLMs (large language models) are AI
systems trained on text and code, used directly as a chatbot. AI software refers to the specialized tools built on top of these systems, such as documentation
search, code execution and image generation. The frontier combines tasks reachable by AI software (roughly 66%, following Eloundou et al.), with an additional
layer of robotics deemed commercially viable by 2040, including autonomous trucking, warehouse and factory automation, construction and agriculture,
bringing the total to 72%. Tasks requiring a general-purpose humanoid robot are excluded. Occupations reflect major U.S. groups, weighted by each
occupation’s share of total U.S. wages. What might lie ahead? Forecasting productivity is difficult even in ordinary times, and profound technological change makes the challenge even greater. Our updated methodology should offer a solid framework from which to reason and refine as new evidence develops. For total factor productivity, we focus on the specific tasks AI can perform, and how efficiently. We then map those gains across the economy, an approach grounded in Hulten’s theorem as applied by Daron Acemoglu and others.[6] We estimate capital deepening by projecting how AI-related investment affects the economy’s productive capital stock, net of depreciation and “crowding out” (displacing other productive investments). By 2040, we believe, AI adoption will have shifted to more embedded agentic,[7] and even robotic, workflows, spreading beyond knowledge-intensive early users to routine work across sectors. But diffusion will be gradual. We expect a slow start, with adoption accelerating in the early 2030s and then tapering as remaining use cases become harder or less economically attractive. Scaling AI will require integrating with legacy systems and redesigning operating models. Friction may be most acute where oversight and liability management require human involvement, particularly where AI missteps could prove costly. This gradual pace is an important premise of our macroeconomic and asset class assumptions. Steady uptake should limit rapid, economy-wide job displacement and keep broad inflation contained, even as the build-out strains supply chains in the near term. In our base case, AI boosts U.S. TFP growth above its pre-AI trend by roughly 40bps, to 1.2% annually,[8] and it lifts U.S. capital stock growth by about 30bps, to 2.3% per year. Together, this raises our total U.S. labor productivity forecast by 50bps vs. our pre-AI baseline, to 2.2%. Small gains compound: A sustained 50bps boost over 15 years would make the U.S. economy 7%–8% larger than it otherwise would have been. Given this is our fourth year incorporating AI into our assumptions, this year’s incremental productivity lift vs. last year is 20bps. Relative to other forecasts, our view appears cautiously optimistic. The 40bps AI-driven TFP uplift exceeds the Congressional Budget Office’s more conservative 10bps estimate while landing in the lower half of the OECD’s 27bps to 85bps scenario range.[9] Against that backdrop, our analysis first builds a baseline forecast for the U.S., then extends it globally, accounting for regional variation. Beyond TFP, our outlook hinges on how much the surge in AI spending ultimately increases productivity. Since 2023, AI demand and enthusiasm have driven U.S. hyperscalers to cumulatively invest close to USD 1.6 trillion in capex, spanning data centers, power, semiconductors and networking. Globally, the total exceeds USD 2 trillion over the same period.[13] Our outlook for capital deepening builds on four factors: the path of AI spending, its composition, the rate of depreciation and the extent to which it crowds out other productive capex. Broadly, the first two variables are additive to growth, while the latter two detract. Developed markets appear better positioned to deploy AI at scale, given their large service sectors, strong digital infrastructure and supportive institutions. Where workforces are shrinking – from Japan and China to the U.S., Germany and Italy – firms will have a greater incentive to use AI to help offset demographic challenges. But economic gains will vary between AI enablers, which supply key inputs for the build-out, and adopters, which successfully integrate AI (Exhibit 2). The two can be mutually reinforcing: Better tools and infrastructure can speed up adoption, and durable monetization can incentivize further investment. Source: Eloundou et al. (2024), International Monetary Fund, J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The IMF AI Preparedness Index scores countries’ AI adoption
readiness across digital infrastructure, human capital, innovation and regulation (0 to 1, rescaled to 0 to 100). Task exposure is the estimated share of work
tasks AI could perform based on each country’s occupation mix, building on the approach of Eloundou et al. with an added robotics layer. The U.S. leads as both an enabler and an adopter, registering the largest AI-driven TFP boost in our forecast universe. Its concentration of frontier model developers, hyperscalers and software platforms is unmatched. Corporate America also has the financial strength and appetite to sustain the AI build-out, supported by a flexible, innovation-oriented business environment. Meanwhile, Europe’s early AI gains skew toward a few key enablers in areas where it has outsize global influence, notably semiconductor manufacturing equipment and power grid and infrastructure. Broader gains should follow as AI diffuses across Europe’s services-heavy economies (several of which are more AI-exposed than the U.S.). However, its fragmentated single market, legal and regulatory burdens, labor constraints and energy supply vulnerabilities may slow AI’s rollout. China is building a parallel AI ecosystem, with homegrown models, domestic chip production and a push into robotics. China’s cost competitiveness may prove an advantage, while deployment of AI (which is often state-mandated) across industrial and consumer sectors could drive economy-level productivity gains. Chinese models are also gaining traction globally, recently overtaking U.S. models in token usage on OpenRouter, a widely used developer gateway. Still, weaker monetization by Chinese firms and export controls on advanced U.S. chips should restrain investment and development. Taiwan and South Korea should continue to benefit from their central role in global tech supply chains, notably in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Both economies rank among the largest upward revisions to our GDP growth assumptions. That competitive position is a strength but also a risk, as economic nationalism and geopolitical uncertainty drive the U.S. and China toward onshore alternatives. Finally, Japan arguably has the strongest incentive to adopt AI, given its aging workforce, but long-tenure norms may hinder diffusion. Our base case is just one plausible path among many alternate scenarios (Exhibits 3A and 3B). AI could disappoint if regulation or social backlash restrains adoption, or if capex resets more sharply due to obsolescence, margin pressure, tighter financing or power constraints. Even with broad diffusion, AI may still underdeliver if oversight adds more work, time savings shift to leisure rather than new tasks, or skill gaps and worker preferences become binding constraints. Such a downside scenario could see AI reach only a quarter of tasks by 2040 (vs. 40% in our base case) and annual TFP growth settle below 1%. Source: J.P. Morgan Asset Management; LHS: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald TFP series) for historical data, RHS: company reports. Total factor productivity is for the private nonfarm business sector, 10-year trailing average of annual growth rates. The capex outlook anchors to reported and projected capex from the top five U.S. hyperscalers, with additional assumptions for neocloud, enterprise and government AI infrastructure. Despite the profound impact AI has already had on markets, we don’t think its potential is fully appreciated. Investors will seek to identify where value accrues, whether through profit growth, risk premia or pricing power. We believe portfolios can best capture that potential by balancing exposure across the AI value chain and funding cycle, spanning public and private markets. That calls for strategic discipline and tactical flexibility. Returns have so far favored the AI enablers. But the set of beneficiaries already extends beyond hyperscalers and semiconductors into infrastructure and power. As adoption spreads, more sectors should participate. This expectation underpins our view that equities will deliver stronger, broader earnings growth and sustain structurally higher margins and valuations than they would have in a world without AI. title: RIOT Stock Gains After Jefferies Upgrade, JP Morgan Price Target Hike: Analysts See Favorable Economics In Corsicana Data Center Deal - TradingView
content: Riot Platforms (RIOT) shares rose in early-morning trade on Tuesday after major updates from Jefferies and JPMorgan. Jefferies upgraded RIOT to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold’ and hiked its price target to $28 from $13, according to CNBC. Meanwhile, JPMorgan analyst Richard Choe also lifted his price target to $28 from $22 and maintained an ‘Overweight’ rating, according to TheFly. Both analysts said Riot had secured the Corsicana lease at attractive risk-adjusted economics. “The powered land lease lets RIOT monetize the site with less execution and financing risk,” Jefferies wrote. RIOT stock rose around 2% in pre-market trade and was among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Retail sentiment around the former Bitcoin miner trended in ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past day, alongside ‘extremely high’ levels of chatter. “We see RIOT’s Corsicana deal as a reset for the market,” Jefferies wrote in its note. “Pairing ready power with the tenant’s modular solution improves speed to market, while the powered-land structure reduces RIOT’s capital needs and shifts meaningful execution risk to the tenant.” Meanwhile, JPMorgan noted that the agreement covers more computing capacity than investors had anticipated and said the 910 megawatts (MW) of IT capacity was “notably larger” than the 756 MW previously expected at the site. The new $28 price target implies about 59% upside from Riot’s Monday closing price. It’s slightly below the average price target of $31.16 cited by Koyfin, implying potential upside of 76%. Of the 22 analysts covering Riot in Koyfin’s survey, 21 rate the stock ‘Strong Buy’ or ‘Buy’, while one has a ‘Hold’ rating. RIOT stock rose about 4% over the past year. Riot announced last week that it will lease its entire Corsicana campus to an unnamed AI developer, which it described as “a leading Frontier AI Lab,” for 15 years. The tenant will pay about $28 billion over the lease’s initial term, making it the largest lease in Riot’s history. The data center capacity is scheduled to come online in stages between September 2027 and July 2028. Including an earlier agreement with the same AI lab at Riot’s Rockdale campus in Texas, along with a contract with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), the company now has about $38 billion in contracted data center revenue. Riot estimates the project will cost about $6 million per MW, roughly half the cost of a typical high-end data center, according to the company. It also said it does not currently expect to issue new shares to finance the projects it has announced. Riot built its business around mining Bitcoin (BTC), which gave it access to large sites with substantial electricity capacity. It is now seeking to monetize that infrastructure by leasing space and power to AI and data center operators. Of late, the company has been increasingly selling Bitcoin from its balance sheet. Riot sold 8,962 BTC last week and had also sold about 4,300 BTC in October. CoinGecko data showed the company held approximately 2,418 BTC, worth about $180 million, at the time of writing. Other bitcoin miners moving into AI didn’t fare as well with analysts on Tuesday. Citi lowered its price target on TeraWulf (WULF) to $24 from $31 while maintaining a ‘Buy’ rating. WULF stock traded flat in pre-market trade. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TeraWulf remained in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, accompanied by ‘high’ levels of chatter. Meanwhile, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Chris Brendler cut his price target on MARA Holdings (MARA) to $11 from $15, while keeping a ‘Buy’ rating. Brendler said MARA’s third-quarter (Q3) results were more important for what they revealed about the company’s balance sheet than its mining performance. He cited market conditions for the price target cut. MARA stock fell about 1.6% in premarket trading. Retail sentiment around the company on Stocktwits shifted to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ over the past day, while chatter increased to ‘high’ from normal’ levels. content: Tronox TROX jumped 7.2% in Monday's trading as J.P. Morgan upgraded the titanium dioxide pigment manufacturer to Neutral from Underweight, even as demand for TiO2 is constrained by negative paint industry volumes in the U.S. and Europe, and the industry is oversupplied. However, J.P. Morgan analyst Jeffrey Zekauskas said he withdrew his price target for Tronox TROX given uncertain and negative business conditions in the context of the quality of the company’s long-term business franchise in a lower interest rate and raw materials environment. Demand conditions are difficult and costs are rising, and 2027 may provide an environment in which prices and volumes in titanium dioxide are at best flat, the analyst said, forecasting Tronox's TROX free cash flow likely will be negative by ~$40M in 2026 excluding dividends and by $72M including dividends, adding that cash flows were assisted in 2026 by a ~$70M working capital benefit, which is not expected to recur in 2027. China's TiO2 export shipments to India are higher by 46% YTD, and China shipments to Europe are nearly 25% higher despite high tariffs; however, India has newly placed tariffs on Chinese product, which Zekauskas said should provide Tronox TROX and Chemours CC with a total volume opportunity of ~200K tons in 2027. Capital concentration, the push toward “sovereign AI,” a complex exit market and a more curated, multi-path route to funding are defining the VC landscape in Europe heading into 2027. European venture capital deal flow has seen an increase this year, reaching €68.4 billion across 7,311 deals in the first nine months of 2026, with €24.6 billion invested in the third quarter alone. At the current investment rate, PitchBook estimates full-year 2026 deal value would represent a 31% year-on-year increase.1 That said, capital is entering a more selective and intensive phase. Larger private rounds, evolving financing needs and a continued private-for-longer environment are changing how companies fund growth, while access to customers, strategic partners and international markets is becoming increasingly important. Here’s a look at the trends shaping European VC in the age of AI. AI-centric companies currently account for 66% of European VC deal value, up from 41% in 2025.³ Interestingly, investors are showing support for funding the infrastructure required to make AI models usable at scale, including compute, orchestration and chips. Additionally, AI companies headquartered in Europe are enjoying a particular tailwind. “AI is the defining theme, but the broader story is how the focus has turned to ‘sovereign’ AI as European governments and corporates view local compute infrastructure, data and AI models as strategic priorities,” said Alex McCracken, co-head of EMEA Venture Capital Coverage at J.P. Morgan. Funding rounds are also happening faster and at higher valuations. Seed and Series A rounds for AI and deep technologies like quantum computing have reached record sizes, and are often pre-empted, widening the divide between perceived category leaders and the rest of the market. The increase in deal sizes reflects sector needs. Defense, robotics, autonomy and deep tech are all areas typically more capital-intensive than legacy software. More than $7.4 billion was deployed into European defense deals in the first three quarters of 2026, compared with $1.5 billion in the same period of 2025. AI investing is entering a more discerning phase. While exposure to the theme itself has attracted significant capital, investors are increasingly differentiating between companies based on sustainable competitive advantages, unit economics and their ability to translate technological innovation into durable revenues. The next phase will be as much about identifying the winners as identifying the right sectors. That capital concentration is contributing to funding bottlenecks, increasing the cost of entry and raising the stakes of investment. “Venture investors can’t afford to miss out of potential AI category leaders in this environment,” McCracken said. “With more capital into fewer companies, investors need greater conviction around whether a business can build a durable competitive advantage and generate huge potential upside to justify that level of investment.” Still, McCracken described the capital-intensive trend as one that requires long-term relationship building. “As capital concentrates, access itself becomes a moat: access to customers, to partners, and to the right capital at the right stage. There’s an opportunity for us to be in the room earlier, helping shape the sequencing,” he said. Despite increased investment, companies face a difficult path to exit. High private-market valuations and substantial capital requirements are narrowing the pool of potential acquirers and complicating the route to liquidity, all while megacap IPO deals dominate headlines. “Public markets are showing encouraging signs of renewed activity, including beyond the largest transactions.,” said Silvia Biscaldi, co-head of EMEA Venture Capital Coverage at J.P. Morgan. “However, investors remain selective, with valuations and the quality of growth increasingly important. The next wave of IPOs will be an important test of how broad and sustainable investor demand really is.” In the meantime, M&A continues to comprise the majority of exits, with acquisitions accounting for 63% of value, up from around 50% last year. 2026 has seen M&A lead deal activity, a slight uptick over previous years. Investors are also proceeding cautiously. With companies staying private longer, investor scrutiny on revenue scale, predictable growth and strong unit economics — for example, profitability per customer or per transaction — raises the bar for consideration. As a result, founders and investors are exploring secondary transactions as an alternative route to liquidity, continuing the elevated activity that defined the first half of 2026. “Secondaries are increasingly becoming a mainstream liquidity tool, enabling existing investors to realize value while allowing companies to continue scaling privately,” said Biscaldi . “This year will have seen the most secondary dealmaking activity in EMEA in several years. We’re already there. The question is, by how much — and can it continue?” Access and stewardship emerge as deal differentiators As a fast-evolving and disruptive technology, AI is providing fertile ground for the creation of new companies and products. In that environment, how founders stand out, and how VC funders connect to them, become just as important as the product or service in development. “As capital becomes more concentrated, conviction needs to be matched by discipline.,” said Biscaldi. “The real differentiator will be which companies can translate technological leadership into commercial scale, and which investors can help them get there.” Access to a robustly funded U.S. market is also a key differentiator for J.P. Morgan’s Venture Capital Coverage team. “For many European founders, the U.S. is not just a funding market, it’s a commercialization market,” said McCracken. “Helping companies bridge that divide is a core part of how we support the ecosystem in a way that benefits everybody: founders, funders and the end user, who winds up with a product or service made better by the relationships we broker.” “As capital becomes more concentrated, conviction needs to be matched by discipline. The real differentiator will be which companies can translate technological leadership into commercial scale, and which investors can help them get there.” Co-head of EMEA Venture Capital Coverage, J.P. Morgan Europe’s venture ecosystem continues to attract capital, but the opportunity is increasingly selective. This is playing out against a backdrop of elevated financing costs, macroeconomic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions and an evolving AI regulatory landscape. For founders, strong management—the “how”— is as important as the “what” that’s being developed. For VCs, the advice is to stay disciplined on valuations in the search for sustainable, high-growth names to support. “The quality bar currently in place is there for a reason,” said McCracken. “For capital-intensive businesses, the priority is to connect technical milestones with commercial progress and a credible path to predictable revenue. Doing so will help determine not simply who can raise capital, but who can turn it into a durable business.” “For many European founders, the U.S. is not just a funding market, it’s a commercialization market.” Co-head of EMEA Venture Capital Coverage, J.P. Morgan Pitchbook, “Q3 2026 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor.” Accessed October 27, 2026. https://pitchbook.com/news/reports/q3-2026-pitchbook-nvca-venture-monitor Venture capital remains concentrated in AI and mega-rounds AI captured 80%+ of venture capital through Q3 2026 while many startups face selective funding. Support aims to help more than 5,000 military-connected entrepreneurs and veteran-owned small businesses with training and resources to access capital, grow their operations, reach new markets, and pursue federal contracts WASHINGTON, November 09, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--JPMorganChase today announced $1.75 million in philanthropic support to help veterans, military spouses, and veteran-owned small businesses strengthen their operations, compete for corporate and government contracts, and grow. The grants will support: Expanding entrepreneurship programs through the D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families (IVMF) at Syracuse University to help entrepreneurs prepare to access capital, grow their operations, and pursue new markets and contracting opportunities, with a goal of serving 5,000 entrepreneurs; Helping veteran-owned small businesses build the skills to compete for and win federal contracts by enabling the National Veteran Small Business Coalition (NVSBC) to develop a first-of-its-kind professional certification for small business government contracting. The announcement was made during the kickoff of National Veterans Small Business Week at JPMorganChase's Bowen Building in Washington, D.C., alongside the U.S. Small Business Administration, D'Aniello IVMF, members of the administration and other policymakers, and veteran-owned small businesses. The event highlighted new opportunities for veteran and military spouse entrepreneurs and business owners to access capital, compete for contracts, and grow. The funding announced today advances that work beyond the event. The new funding builds on JPMorganChase's longstanding support for veterans and military families. The firm is a founding sponsor of D'Aniello IVMF and, 15 years ago, helped launch the Veteran Jobs Mission, part of its broader work to expand business and career opportunities for the military-connected community. "Veterans and military spouses bring experience, leadership, and drive to building their businesses, but those strengths are only part of what it takes to grow. Access to the right guidance, networks, and opportunities can make a real difference," said Tim Berry, Global Head of Corporate Responsibility and Chairman of the Mid-Atlantic Region at JPMorganChase. "By supporting organizations with deep expertise in the military-connected community, we're helping these entrepreneurs grow their businesses, reach new customers, and compete for contracts. This work builds on our longstanding support for veterans and military families and our broader efforts to expand economic opportunity through our American Dream Initiative." Helping veteran entrepreneurs start, grow, and reach new markets The U.S. is home to approximately 1.9 million veteran-owned businesses that employ approximately 5.5 million people. Helping them grow takes more than capital; it takes practical guidance, connections, and access to new markets. The grants announced today bring together support at different stages of the business journey, from early training and mentorship to business-growth programs and federal contracting education: D'Aniello IVMF: Continued support to expand entrepreneurship programs that aim to serve 5,000 entrepreneurs, helping veteran- and military spouse-owned businesses prepare to access capital, strengthen and scale their operations, reach new markets, and compete for contracts to drive revenue growth and job creation. Since its inception, D'Aniello IVMF has supported more than 235,000 military-connected individuals, and its entrepreneurship alumni businesses have reported more than $4.8 billion in combined annual revenue and support more than 52,000 jobs. JPMorganChase is a founding sponsor of D'Aniello IVMF, and the organizations also work together through CEOcircle, which connects business owners with peer networks, mentorship, business expertise, and dedicated banking liaisons. More than 250 business leaders have participated in CEOcircle since the partnership launched in 2021, with scaling businesses generating more than $1.79 billion in revenue and creating more than 6,300 jobs. NVSBC: Support to develop a first-of-its-kind professional certification for small business government contracting, building on work that has already helped nearly 2,000 veteran-owned small businesses build the knowledge, skills, and resources needed to access the federal marketplace and compete for and secure government contracts. Among businesses that completed the pilot program, 55% reported increased revenue and nearly 40% reported securing at least one government contract. Together, the programs pair access to capital with practical guidance, training, mentorship, and connections so veteran entrepreneurs and military families can navigate the challenges of business ownership with a stronger support system. "For veteran-owned small businesses, federal contracting can be an important path to growth, but knowing how to compete in that marketplace is critical," said Scott Jensen, Chief Executive Officer of the National Veteran Small Business Coalition. "We've already seen the difference this training can make, with participating businesses reporting increased revenue and new contract wins. With JPMorganChase's support, we can expand that work and help more veteran entrepreneurs build the skills they need to compete." "Veteran and military spouse entrepreneurs need access to business support at every stage, from launching a company to sustaining its growth. Strong partners are essential to an ecosystem that can meet those evolving needs," said Barb Carson, Managing Director of Programs and Policy at Syracuse University's D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families (IVMF). "JPMorganChase's longstanding commitment has supported the D'Aniello IVMF in continuing to build a strong network, bringing together funding, business expertise and connections to new markets." Building on 15 years of support for the military-connected community Veterans and military spouses offer adaptability, resilience, and a strong sense of service—qualities that strengthen our workforce. JPMorganChase is dedicated to helping them translate their experiences into meaningful careers. From 2020 through 2026, JPMorganChase contributed more than $16 million to organizations serving veterans and the military community. This year marks 15 years since JPMorganChase established its Office of Military & Veterans Affairs and helped launch the Veteran Jobs Mission, advancing the firm's efforts to expand employment opportunities for veterans and military spouses. The Veteran Jobs Mission has grown from 11 companies in 2011 to more than 315 today and has surpassed one million U.S. veteran hires, with JPMorganChase hiring approximately 21,000 veterans and employing more than 3,100 military spouses. The firm also supports military-connected talent through programs including the Military Pathways Development Program, which provides veterans with training and mentorship through two, one-year rotational roles, and its Virtual Call Center program, which creates flexible customer-service career opportunities for talent who may have limited access to traditional call center sites, including military spouses. Operating in Detroit, Baltimore, Atlanta, and Tucson, the Virtual Call Center program has created more than 450 U.S. jobs with competitive pay, benefits, and career advancement opportunities. For military spouses, the program offers full-time roles that can move with them when their families relocate. Advancing the American Dream for small business owners The new support complements JPMorganChase's American Dream Initiative, a multi-year effort to help expand economic opportunity by accelerating and scaling effective solutions. The initiative includes a firmwide effort to reach as many as 10 million small businesses nationwide, up from more than seven million served today, with expanded banker presence and access to the capital, coaching, tools, and practical policy support they need to thrive. title: DTE sells non-utility DTE Vantage business to J.P Morgan - Daily Energy Insider
content: DTE Energy is selling its non-utility DTE Vantage business for approximately $3 billion to institutional investors advised by the Global Infrastructure group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The transaction advances DTE’s long-term strategy and continued focus on customer affordability, while strengthening its ability to make significant utility investments. To the latter point, it will support a substantial increase in investment in the electric and gas utilities, which will total approximately $44 billion over the next five years. This includes investment to serve growing data center demand. “DTE Vantage has been a strong non-utility business and valued part of DTE Energy for more than 30 years,” Joi Harris, DTE president and CEO, said. “This transaction advances our strategy to focus our resources on our regulated electric and gas utilities, where we see significant opportunities to invest on behalf of customers and communities. The sale supports our plan to deliver meaningful affordability benefits for customers, strengthens our ability to execute a substantial utility investment plan and positions DTE as a high-growth, premium utility with a stronger long-term outlook.” The sale includes the sale of primarily all DTE Vantage assets, except EES Coke. The company has invested nearly $4.1 billion in its utilities through the third quarter and remains on track to invest $6.1 billion this year. The capital investments are strengthening and modernizing the company’s electric and natural gas systems and supporting the transition to cleaner power generation. Lazard is acting as exclusive financial advisor to DTE Energy, and Kirkland & Ellis is acting as legal advisor to DTE Energy. The sale is expected to close in the first half of 2027. DTE Energy, based in Detroit, serves 2.3 million electric customers in Southeast Michigan and 1.4 million natural gas customers across Michigan.
